title: Under the Hood of a Write
summary: Pulsewise fitness bands stream 40,000 heart-rate samples a second. Follow one write into the storage engine: the write-ahead log, B-trees that update in place, and LSM-trees that never do.

goals.text: Explain why a write-ahead log makes acknowledged writes survive a crash
See how a B-tree updates pages in place, and why that means random I/O
Follow an LSM-tree write: memtable, flush, SSTables, compaction
Compare read and write amplification of both engines

steps.title: What happens after INSERT?
body: Pulsewise makes fitness bands. Every band uploads heart-rate samples, and the ingest API stores about 40,000 samples a second, each roughly 100 bytes.

To the API, storing a sample is one INSERT and an “OK”. Inside the database a storage engine decides how those bytes reach the disk — and that choice sets how fast writes go, how fast reads go, and what survives a crash.

steps.title: Fast — until the power cuts
body: The quickest engine imaginable changes the data in memory, replies “OK”, and copies memory to disk every few seconds. RAM is thousands of times faster than disk, so it flies.

Then a power cut hits. Everything written since the last copy — samples the API already confirmed — is gone. A database that forgets acknowledged writes isn't durable, and durability is the D in ACID.

callout.text: “OK” must mean “safe on disk”. If it only means “in memory”, the client has no idea which data to send again.

card.title: What the crash took
lines: 14:02:00  last flush to disk
14:02:08  power cut
! 8 s × 40,000 samples = 320,000 acked writes gone
# they were only ever in RAM

steps.title: Write-ahead log: append, then ack
body: Before touching any data page, the engine appends a short record describing the change to the end of a write-ahead log (WAL) and forces it to disk with fsync. Only then does it update the page in memory and reply.

Appending to the end of one file is the cheapest thing a disk can do. Pages are written back later in bulk (a checkpoint); after a crash, the engine replays the log from the last checkpoint and nothing acknowledged is lost.
changes: ~ Buffer pool back, flushed at checkpoints

card.title: Write-ahead log
lines: 1. append the change to the end of the log
2. fsync — the bytes are on disk
3. apply to the page in RAM, then ack
= crash? replay the log since the last checkpoint
# one fsync can cover thousands of writes (group commit)

steps.title: B-tree engines update pages in place
body: Most relational databases keep table and index data in B-trees made of fixed-size pages (often 8 KB). Every key has exactly one home page; a write modifies that page in memory and the checkpoint writes the page back to the same spot on disk.
Reads love this: any key is a root-to-leaf walk of 3–4 pages, most of them cached. Writes pay: samples from different bands land in pages scattered across the disk.
changes: ~ Checkpoint writes pages back in place

card.title: B-tree: update in place
lines: each row lives in exactly one 8 KB page
a write dirties that page in RAM
checkpoint writes the page back to its own spot
= reads: root → branch → leaf, 3–4 pages
! pages are scattered → random disk writes

steps.title: Three times the bands, a random-write wall
body: A holiday sale triples the bands: 120,000 samples a second. Each sample touches a different page, so the checkpoint has to rewrite thousands of scattered 8 KB pages to persist a few hundred bytes in each.

That ratio — bytes the disk writes per byte you asked to store — is write amplification. The disk saturates on random writes, checkpoints fall behind, and the engine tops out near 52,000 samples a second.

lines: # random keys: neighbours in a page rarely change together

steps.title: LSM-tree: buffer, sort, write once
body: A log-structured merge-tree never updates data in place. Each write goes to the WAL (for durability) and into a memtable, an in-memory structure kept sorted by key.

When the memtable reaches ~64 MB it is written out in one go as a sorted, immutable file — an SSTable — and a fresh memtable starts. Every disk write is now a long sequential stream, so the same disk keeps up with all 120,000 samples a second.

card.title: LSM-tree: never overwrite
lines: writes go to the log and a sorted in-memory table
full memtable → written out as one sorted file
files (SSTables) are immutable once written
= the disk only ever sees long sequential writes

steps.title: Reads have more places to look
body: A key may have been written many times, so its newest value could be in the memtable or in any SSTable. A read checks the memtable, then files from newest to oldest, and stops at the first hit.

To avoid opening every file, each SSTable carries a bloom filter — a tiny bit-array that answers “definitely not here” or “maybe here”. Most files are ruled out in memory, so a typical read touches one or two files.

callout.text: Bloom filters can say “maybe” wrongly (a false positive costs one wasted read) but never say “no” when the key is there.

changes: + Bloom filter verdict on each file

lines: 1. memtable (newest data)
2. SSTables, newest → oldest, until found
# each file keeps a bloom filter: “definitely not here” or “maybe”
= most files are skipped without touching disk
! more files → more places to look

steps.title: Compaction tidies up
body: Left alone, SSTables pile up: reads slow down and old versions of overwritten or deleted keys waste disk. In the background, compaction merge-sorts several files into one, keeping only the newest value of each key and dropping deleted ones.

Merging sorted files is sequential too, but it rewrites the same data again and again as it moves into bigger files. That's the LSM's own write amplification — paid in the background instead of on the write path.

callout.text: If compaction can't keep up with writes, files accumulate and read latency creeps up. Leave disk bandwidth headroom for it.

changes: ~ Old SSTables fade out after compaction

card.title: Compaction, in the background
lines: merge-sort several files into one
keep only the newest value of each key
drop deleted keys (tombstones)
= fewer files per read, less wasted space
! the same bytes get rewritten many times

Pulsewise keeps user profiles (read-heavy, updated rarely) in a B-tree database and the sample stream (write-heavy, read by time range) in an LSM-based store.

steps.title: Every write, step by step
body:
• A write is acknowledged only after its WAL record is on disk — that's durability.
  • B-trees update fixed pages in place: cheap, predictable reads; random writes.
  • LSM-trees buffer in a sorted memtable and flush immutable SSTables: sequential writes; reads check several files, helped by bloom filters.
  • Compaction keeps LSM reads fast, at the cost of rewriting data in the background.
